questions.text: The SI unit of electric charge is the:
questions.explanation: The SI unit of electric charge is the Coulomb (C), defined via the ampere: 1 C = 1 A·s.

questions.text: The charge of one electron is approximately:
questions.explanation: The electron carries a negative charge of magnitude e = 1.6022 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

questions.text: Coulomb's constant k is equal to:
questions.explanation: Coulomb's constant k = 1/(4πε₀) = 8.9876 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².

questions.text: Two charges of +3 μC and -3 μC are separated by 12 cm. The magnitude of the force between them is approximately:
When two charges have opposite signs, the electrostatic force between them is:
questions.explanation: Opposite charges attract each other according to Coulomb's Law.

questions.text: If the distance between two point charges is doubled, the electrostatic force between them:
questions.explanation: F ∝ 1/r². If r doubles, F decreases by a factor of 4.

questions.text: The permittivity of free space ε₀ has a value of:
questions.explanation: ε₀ = 8.85419 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²), also written as F/m.

questions.text: Electric charge is quantized. This means:
questions.explanation: All observed charges are integer multiples of e = 1.6022 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
options: Charge only exists in multiples of the elementary charge e

questions.text: The mass of an electron is approximately:
questions.explanation: The electron mass mₑ = 9.1094 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

questions.text: Two identical conducting spheres attract each other with force F. When connected by a wire and separated, they:
questions.explanation: The wire equalizes the total charge between the spheres. If the original charges had opposite signs, the new equal charges will repel.

questions.text: The principle of superposition states that the total force on a charge is:
questions.explanation: Electric forces obey superposition; the net force is the vector sum of all individual Coulomb forces.
options: The vector sum of individual forces
The scalar sum of individual forces
Equal to the largest individual force

questions.text: To maximize the repulsive force when dividing a charge Q into two parts, each part should be:
questions.explanation: F = k(Q-q)q/r². Maximizing with dF/dq = 0 gives q = Q/2.

questions.text: The electric field E is defined as:
questions.explanation: The electric field at a point is the force per unit charge: E = F/q₀.

questions.text: The SI unit of electric field is:
questions.explanation: Electric field has units of force per charge: N/C (also equivalent to V/m).

questions.text: The electric field due to a point charge q at distance r is:
questions.explanation: From Coulomb's Law, E = kq/r², pointing radially away from positive charges.

questions.text: Electric field lines originate on:
questions.explanation: Electric field lines originate on positive charges and terminate on negative charges.

questions.text: The electric field inside a uniform infinite sheet of charge with surface charge density σ is:
questions.explanation: For an infinite sheet, E = σ/(2ε₀) on each side of the sheet.

questions.text: An electric dipole consists of:
questions.explanation: An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance.
options: Two opposite charges ±q separated by distance d

questions.text: The electric dipole moment p has magnitude:
questions.explanation: The dipole moment magnitude is p = qd, where d is the separation between the charges.

questions.text: When an electric dipole is placed in a uniform electric field, it experiences:
questions.explanation: In a uniform field, the net force on a dipole is zero but there is a torque τ = p × E.

questions.text: The torque on an electric dipole in a uniform field E is:
questions.explanation: The torque on a dipole is τ = p × E, with magnitude pE sinθ.

questions.text: The potential energy of a dipole in an electric field is:
questions.explanation: The potential energy is U = -p·E = -pE cosθ.

questions.text: The electric field on the axis of a ring of charge with total charge q, radius R, at distance z from center is:
questions.explanation: This is the standard result for the axial field of a uniformly charged ring.

questions.text: Field lines cannot cross one another because:
questions.explanation: If field lines crossed, the electric field at that point would have two directions simultaneously, which is impossible.
options: The field is always zero where they cross
At any point, the field has a unique direction

questions.text: An object with charge 24 μC is placed in a uniform electric field of 610 N/C directed vertically. The object 'floats' when its mass is approximately:
The linear charge density λ has SI units of:
questions.explanation: Linear charge density λ = charge per unit length, with units C/m.

questions.text: The surface charge density σ has SI units of:
questions.explanation: Surface charge density σ = charge per unit area, with units C/m².

questions.text: For a charged disk of radius R and surface charge density σ, the field at distance z on its axis is:
questions.explanation: This is derived by integrating the ring formula over the disk radius.

questions.text: Gauss's Law relates the electric flux through a closed surface to:
questions.explanation: Gauss's Law: Φ = ∮E·dA = q_enc/ε₀.
options: The total charge outside the surface
The total charge enclosed by the surface
The electric field at the surface

questions.text: Electric flux has SI units of:
questions.explanation: Electric flux = E × Area has units of (N/C)(m²) = N·m²/C.

questions.text: The electric field inside a hollow spherically symmetric shell of charge is:
questions.explanation: Inside a hollow shell, q_enc = 0, so by Gauss's Law E = 0.

questions.text: For a Gaussian surface, the area vector dA points:
questions.explanation: For closed surfaces, the convention is that dA points outward (away from the enclosed volume).

questions.text: The electric field just outside a conducting surface with charge density σ is:
questions.explanation: Just outside a conductor E = σ/ε₀, perpendicular to the surface.

questions.text: In electrostatics, the electric field inside a conductor is:
questions.explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside any conductor is zero.

questions.text: For a line charge with linear charge density λ, the electric field at perpendicular distance r is:
questions.explanation: Using a cylindrical Gaussian surface gives E = λ/(2πε₀r).

questions.text: If a conductor carries a net charge, where does this charge reside?
questions.explanation: Any excess charge on a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium resides entirely on the surface.

questions.text: A Gaussian surface is a:
questions.explanation: A Gaussian surface is any closed surface chosen for applying Gauss's Law.

questions.text: An isolated conductor has a net charge of +10 μC and contains a cavity with a charge q = +3 μC inside. The charge on the outer surface is:
questions.explanation: Inner surface gets -3 μC to shield the cavity. Outer surface = +10 μC - (-3 μC) = +13 μC.

questions.text: The electric flux through a closed surface that encloses no charge is:
questions.explanation: By Gauss's Law: Φ = q_enc/ε₀ = 0 when no charge is enclosed.

questions.text: For a uniformly charged solid sphere of total charge q and radius R, the field at r > R is:
questions.explanation: Outside a spherical charge distribution, E = kq/r² (same as a point charge at center).

questions.text: Capacitance is defined as:
questions.explanation: Capacitance C = q/V, where q is charge and V is the potential difference.

questions.text: The SI unit of capacitance is the:
questions.explanation: 1 farad = 1 F = 1 C/V.

questions.text: For a parallel-plate capacitor with plate area A and separation d, the capacitance is:
questions.explanation: The parallel-plate capacitor formula is C = ε₀A/d.

questions.text: When capacitors are connected in parallel, the equivalent capacitance is:
questions.explanation: Parallel capacitors add directly: C_eq = C₁ + C₂ + C₃ + ...
options: C_eq = product of all C divided by sum

questions.text: When capacitors are connected in series, the equivalent capacitance satisfies:
questions.explanation: Series capacitors: 1/C_eq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + 1/C₃ + ...

questions.text: Energy stored in a capacitor is:
questions.explanation: Energy stored: U = q²/(2C) = ½CV² = qV/2.

questions.text: A dielectric material inserted between capacitor plates:
questions.explanation: C = κC_air, where κ is the dielectric constant (κ > 1 for all dielectrics).

questions.text: The energy density of an electric field is:
questions.explanation: Energy density in an electric field: u = ½ε₀E².

questions.text: For capacitors in series, the charge on each capacitor is:
questions.explanation: In series, the same charge q accumulates on each capacitor.

questions.text: For capacitors in parallel, the voltage across each capacitor is:
questions.explanation: In parallel, all capacitors share the same potential difference.

questions.text: A 25 μF capacitor is charged by a 120 V battery. The charge on it is:
The equivalent capacitance of 10 μF and 5 μF in series is:
The capacitance of a cylindrical capacitor with inner radius a and outer radius b, length L is:
questions.explanation: The cylindrical capacitor formula is C = 2πε₀L/ln(b/a).

questions.text: For resistors in series, the equivalent capacitance is always _______ any individual capacitance.
questions.explanation: For capacitors in series, C_eq is always less than any individual capacitor.

questions.text: Ohm's Law states:
questions.explanation: Ohm's Law: Voltage = Current × Resistance (V = IR).

questions.text: The SI unit of resistance is the:
questions.explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω), where 1 Ω = 1 V/A.

questions.text: Electric current is defined as:
questions.explanation: Current I = Q/t, the rate of flow of charge.

questions.text: Voltage is defined as:
questions.explanation: Voltage (potential difference) V = W/Q, energy per unit charge.

questions.text: Resistance of a conductor depends on:
questions.explanation: R = ρL/A, where ρ depends on material and temperature.

questions.text: The formula for resistance in terms of resistivity ρ is:
questions.explanation: R = ρL/A, where ρ is resistivity, L is length, A is cross-sectional area.

questions.text: For resistors in series, the equivalent resistance is:
questions.explanation: Series resistors add directly: R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + ...

questions.text: For resistors in parallel, the equivalent resistance satisfies:
questions.explanation: Parallel resistors: 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ + ...

questions.text: Kirchhoff's Junction Rule states:
questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL): ΣI_in = ΣI_out (conservation of charge).
options: Sum of voltages around a loop = 0
Sum of currents entering = sum leaving a junction

questions.text: Kirchhoff's Loop Rule states:
questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL): The algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero.

questions.text: Power dissipated in a resistor is:
questions.explanation: P = IV = I²R = V²/R — all three are equivalent expressions for power.

questions.text: In a series circuit, the current through each element is:
questions.explanation: In series, the same current flows through all elements.

questions.text: In a parallel circuit, the voltage across each element is:
questions.explanation: In parallel, all elements share the same potential difference.

questions.text: For resistors in parallel, the equivalent resistance is always:
questions.explanation: R_eq for parallel resistors is always less than any individual resistance.
options: Less than the smallest individual resistance

questions.text: A 16 V source is connected across a 2 kΩ resistor. The current is:
The conventional current direction is:
questions.explanation: Conventional current flows from + to - terminal outside the source (opposite to electron flow).
options: From positive to negative terminal through external circuit
In the direction of electron flow

questions.text: Two 100 Ω bulbs connected in parallel across 24 V are ________ than when connected in series.
questions.explanation: Parallel: P = V²/R = 576/100 = 5.76 W each. Series: P = I²R = (0.12)²(100) = 1.44 W each.

questions.text: The first band of a 4-band resistor color code represents:
questions.explanation: In a 4-band code: Band 1 = first digit, Band 2 = second digit, Band 3 = multiplier, Band 4 = tolerance.

questions.text: A resistor with color bands Brown-Black-Brown-Gold has a resistance of:
questions.explanation: Brown=1, Black=0, Brown=×10, Gold=±5%. So 10 × 10 = 100 Ω ±5%.

questions.text: Gold as the 4th band of a resistor indicates a tolerance of:
questions.explanation: Gold tolerance band = ±5%, Silver = ±10%, no band = ±20%.

questions.text: The force on a moving charge in a magnetic field is given by:
questions.explanation: The magnetic (Lorentz) force is F = q(v × B), with magnitude F = qvB sinθ.

questions.text: The SI unit of magnetic field (magnetic flux density) is the:
questions.explanation: The SI unit of B-field is the Tesla (T), where 1 T = 1 kg/(A·s²).

questions.text: A positive charge moving to the right in a magnetic field pointing out of the page experiences a force directed:
questions.explanation: Using F = qv × B: v = +x̂, B = +ẑ, so v×B = x̂×ẑ = -ŷ (downward) for positive q.

questions.text: The magnetic force on a stationary charge in a magnetic field is:
questions.explanation: F = qv × B. If v = 0, then F = 0. Magnetic force requires motion.

questions.text: A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences:
questions.explanation: When v is parallel to B, the angle θ = 0°, so F = qvB sin(0°) = 0.

questions.text: The radius of circular motion of a charge q, mass m, speed v in magnetic field B is:
questions.explanation: Setting qvB = mv²/r and solving: r = mv/(qB).

questions.text: The magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor in a uniform field B is:
questions.explanation: Force on current-carrying wire: F = IL × B, with magnitude ILB sinθ.

questions.text: The Biot-Savart Law gives the magnetic field due to:
questions.explanation: The Biot-Savart Law: dB = (μ₀/4π)(Idl × r̂/r²) gives field from a current element.

questions.text: The permeability of free space μ₀ has a value of:
questions.explanation: μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A is the permeability of free space.

questions.text: The magnetic field at distance r from a long straight wire carrying current I is:
questions.explanation: Using Ampere's Law for a long straight wire: B = μ₀I/(2πr).

questions.text: Two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction:
questions.explanation: Parallel currents in the same direction attract; opposite currents repel.

questions.text: Ampere's Law states:
questions.explanation: Ampere's Law: ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enc, relating circulation of B to enclosed current.

questions.text: The magnetic field inside a solenoid with n turns per unit length and current I is:
questions.explanation: Inside a long solenoid: B = μ₀nI, where n = N/L is turns per unit length.

questions.text: Magnetic flux Φ through an area A in a field B is:
questions.explanation: Magnetic flux Φ = B·A = BA cosθ, where θ is the angle between B and the area normal.

questions.text: Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction states that the induced EMF is:
questions.explanation: Faraday's Law: EMF = -dΦ/dt (negative sign from Lenz's Law).
options: Equal to the rate of change of magnetic flux

questions.text: Lenz's Law states that the induced current creates a magnetic field that:
questions.explanation: Lenz's Law: The induced EMF is in a direction to oppose the change that produced it.
options: Is parallel to the original field

questions.text: The Hall Effect occurs when:
questions.explanation: The Hall Effect: moving charges in a conductor in a magnetic field accumulate on one side, creating a transverse voltage.
options: Current flows in a magnetic field, creating a transverse voltage

questions.text: The torque on a magnetic dipole (current loop) in a magnetic field B is:
questions.explanation: Torque on a magnetic dipole: τ = m × B, where m = IA is the magnetic dipole moment.

questions.text: The magnetic field at the center of a circular loop of radius R carrying current I is:
questions.explanation: At the center of a circular loop: B = μ₀I/(2R).

questions.text: Magnetic monopoles:
questions.explanation: Magnetic monopoles have never been observed. The divergence of B is always zero: ∮B·dA = 0.
options: Do not exist; magnets always have two poles

questions.text: The cyclotron frequency of a charged particle in a magnetic field is:
questions.explanation: Cyclotron frequency: f = ω/(2π) = qB/(2πm), independent of particle speed.

questions.text: Materials that are strongly attracted to magnets are called:
questions.explanation: Ferromagnetic materials (Fe, Ni, Co) are strongly attracted to magnets and can be permanently magnetized.

questions.text: Self-inductance L is defined by:
questions.explanation: Self-inductance: EMF = -L(dI/dt), opposing changes in current.

questions.text: The SI unit of inductance is the:
questions.explanation: Inductance is measured in Henry (H), where 1 H = 1 V·s/A.

questions.text: Energy stored in an inductor is:
questions.explanation: Energy stored in an inductor: U = ½LI².

questions.text: The inductance of a solenoid with N turns, length l, and cross-section area A is:
questions.explanation: Solenoid inductance: L = μ₀N²A/l = μ₀n²Al, where n = N/l.

questions.text: The word 'atom' comes from the Greek word 'atomos' which means:
questions.explanation: Democritus coined 'atomos' meaning 'not to be cut' or indivisible.

questions.text: Who first suggested the existence of atoms and coined the name 'atomos'?
questions.explanation: Democritus was the first to suggest the existence of atoms and coined the term atomos.

questions.text: Dalton's atomic theory was developed in:
questions.explanation: J. Dalton developed his famous theory of the atom in 1803.

questions.text: According to Dalton's theory, atoms are:
questions.explanation: Dalton considered atoms as the smallest, dense, hard and indivisible particles.
options: Smallest, dense, hard and indivisible particles

questions.text: A major limitation of Dalton's theory was its failure to explain:
questions.explanation: Dalton's theory fails to explain differences in valency and mass, and cannot account for isotopes and isobars.
options: Why atoms of different kinds differ in valency and mass

questions.text: The electron was discovered by:
questions.explanation: J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 using cathode ray experiments.

questions.text: The cathode ray experiment was performed using a:
questions.explanation: The discharge tube (Crooke's tube) is a glass tube about 60 cm long with two metal electrodes in partial vacuum.
options: Glass tube with two electrodes in partial vacuum

questions.text: In a cathode ray tube, the negative electrode is called:
questions.explanation: The negative electrode is called the cathode; the positive electrode is the anode.

questions.text: Cathode rays travel in:
questions.explanation: One of the key properties of cathode rays is that they travel in straight lines.

questions.text: The charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) of an electron is approximately:
questions.explanation: The charge-to-mass ratio of the electron: e/m = 1.758820 × 10¹¹ C/kg.

questions.text: R.S. Millikan measured the charge on an electron using the:
questions.explanation: Millikan used the famous oil drop experiment to determine the charge on an electron: -1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

questions.text: Cathode rays cause fluorescence because they:
questions.explanation: The kinetic energy of cathode ray electrons causes fluorescence in materials like ZnS.
options: Are fast-moving negatively charged particles that excite fluorescent materials

questions.text: When cathode rays fall on heavy metals, they produce:
questions.explanation: A key property: When cathode rays fall on heavy metals, X-rays are produced.

questions.text: The proton was discovered by:
questions.explanation: The proton was discovered by German scientist Eugen Goldstein through the anode ray (canal ray) experiment in 1886.

questions.text: Anode rays (canal rays) are:
questions.explanation: Anode rays consist of positively charged particles (cations) moving toward the cathode.

questions.text: The e/m ratio of anode rays compared to cathode rays is:
questions.explanation: The e/m ratio of anode rays is less than that of electrons because protons are much heavier.

questions.text: The e/m ratio for anode rays is maximum when the gas in the tube is:
questions.explanation: The e/m ratio is maximum for hydrogen gas because H⁺ (proton) has the lowest mass of any ion.

questions.text: The neutron was discovered by:
questions.explanation: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles.

questions.text: The neutron is a fundamental particle of all atomic nuclei except:
questions.explanation: Protium (ordinary hydrogen ¹H) has no neutrons; it consists only of a proton and an electron.

questions.text: The mass of a proton is approximately:
questions.explanation: Proton mass mₚ = 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1.00757 amu.

questions.text: The ratio of proton mass to electron mass is approximately:
Thomson's atomic model is also known as the:
questions.explanation: Thomson proposed the Plum-Pudding model: a uniform sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it.

questions.text: A major limitation of Thomson's model is that:
questions.explanation: Thomson's model fails because it is static and cannot explain the spectral lines or electron movement.
options: It is a static model that doesn't reflect electron movement
It predicts wrong charge for electrons

questions.text: Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment used:
questions.explanation: Rutherford bombarded a thin gold foil with high-speed alpha particles.
options: Alpha particles hitting a gold foil

questions.text: From Rutherford's experiment, most alpha particles:
questions.explanation: Most alpha particles passed straight through, indicating atoms are mostly empty space.
options: Were absorbed by the gold foil

questions.text: Rutherford's model proposed that positive charge is:
questions.explanation: Rutherford proposed that positive charge (and most mass) is concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus.
options: Concentrated in a tiny dense nucleus

questions.text: The Bohr model was proposed by:
questions.explanation: The Bohr model was presented by Niels Bohr and Ernest Rutherford in 1913.
options: Niels Bohr and Ernest Rutherford in 1913

questions.text: In the Bohr model, electrons:
questions.explanation: Bohr proposed that electrons revolve around the nucleus in specific allowed orbits (shells).
options: Revolve around the nucleus in fixed orbits

questions.text: The Bohr model formula for orbit radius is:
questions.explanation: Bohr radius formula: r = 0.529 × n²/Z Å, where n is principal quantum number and Z is atomic number.

questions.text: The Bohr model is only applicable to:
questions.explanation: Bohr's model is only applicable for one-electron systems like H, He⁺, Li²⁺, etc.

questions.text: De Broglie proposed the concept of dual nature of electrons in:
questions.explanation: De Broglie introduced the concept of dual nature in electrons in 1923, using Einstein's E = mc².

questions.text: De Broglie's relation states that any moving particle has an associated:
questions.explanation: De Broglie proposed that any moving particle or object has an associated wave (matter wave).

questions.text: Schrödinger's electron cloud model was developed in:
questions.explanation: Erwin Schrödinger developed the electron cloud model in 1925, introducing the concept of orbitals.

questions.text: In Schrödinger's model, the regions where electrons are likely to be found are called:
questions.explanation: Schrödinger and Heisenberg determined the regions (orbitals) where electrons would likely be found.

questions.text: The atomic number Z is equal to:
questions.explanation: Atomic number Z = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom.
options: Number of protons (and electrons in neutral atom)

questions.text: The mass number A is defined as:
questions.explanation: Mass number A = number of protons (Z) + number of neutrons (N) = total nucleons.

questions.text: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with:
questions.explanation: Isotopes: same Z (same element/protons), different A (different neutrons).
options: Same mass number, different atomic number
Same atomic number, different mass number

questions.text: An example of isotopes is:
questions.explanation: Protium, deuterium, and tritium are isotopes of hydrogen — same Z=1, different mass numbers.

questions.text: Isobars are atoms with:
questions.explanation: Isobars: same A (same total nucleons), different Z (different elements).
options: Same atomic number, different mass number
Same mass number, different atomic number

questions.text: An example of isobars is:
questions.explanation: ⁴⁰₁₉K and ⁴⁰₂₀Ca are isobars: same mass number (40), different atomic numbers (19 and 20).

questions.text: Isotones are atoms of different elements with:
questions.explanation: Isotones: different elements (different Z) but the same number of neutrons.

questions.text: Isoelectronic species have:
questions.explanation: Isoelectronic atoms/ions/molecules have the same number of electrons (e.g., Cl⁻ and Ar both have 18 e⁻).

questions.text: Which of these pairs is isoelectronic?
questions.explanation: H₂O has 10 electrons; NH₃ also has 10 electrons — they are isoelectronic.

questions.text: Isodiaphers are atoms with the same:
questions.explanation: Isodiaphers have the same value of (n - p), i.e., the same difference between neutron and proton numbers.

questions.text: The nucleus of tritium (³H) contains:
questions.explanation: Tritium ³₁H: Z=1 (1 proton), A=3, so neutrons = 3-1 = 2 neutrons.

questions.text: Johann Balmer derived a formula for predicting the hydrogen spectrum in:
questions.explanation: Johann Balmer derived the formula for predicting the hydrogen spectrum in 1885.

questions.text: The order of specific charge (e/m) from smallest to largest is:
questions.explanation: e/m: neutron (0) < proton (smaller) < electron (largest at 1.76×10¹¹ C/kg).

questions.text: An element has 18 electrons and 20 neutrons. Its mass number is:
questions.explanation: For a neutral atom, protons = electrons = 18. Mass number A = p + n = 18 + 20 = 38.

questions.text: Isosters are molecules that have the same:
questions.explanation: Isosters have the same number of atoms and the same number of electrons (e.g., CO₂ and N₂O).

questions.text: The discovery of neutron was late because neutrons are:
questions.explanation: Neutrons carry no charge, so they are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields, making them hard to detect.
options: Chargeless (not deflected by E or B fields)

questions.text: In nuclear fission, a uranium-238 nucleus splits into two fragments each with 46 protons and radius 5.9×10⁻¹⁵ m. The repulsive force between them is approximately:
The electric field at the center of a square due to four equal positive charges at the corners is:
questions.explanation: By symmetry, equal charges at all four corners produce fields that cancel at the center.
options: Equal to field from one charge

questions.text: The electric field for a planar charge distribution does NOT depend on:
questions.explanation: E = σ/(2ε₀) for an infinite plane — independent of distance from the sheet.

questions.text: To store 1 C of charge with 110 V using 1 μF capacitors in parallel, you need:
Kirchhoff's laws are based on conservation of:
questions.explanation: KCL is based on conservation of charge; KVL is based on conservation of energy.

questions.text: A particle moves in a circle in a magnetic field. Doubling the magnetic field strength:
questions.explanation: r = mv/(qB). If B doubles, r halves (for same mass, charge, and speed).

questions.text: Which particle is NOT a fundamental subatomic particle?
questions.explanation: The three fundamental subatomic particles are the electron, proton, and neutron.

questions.text: The mass of 75.0 kg of electrons contains how many electrons?
An electron released from rest in a uniform field of 2×10⁴ N/C has acceleration:
A spherical Gaussian surface encloses a total charge of 5 nC. The electric flux through it is approximately:
Two capacitors of 2.0 μF and 4.0 μF in parallel across 300 V store total energy of:
A 1.5 A current flows through an 80 Ω resistor. The voltage across it is:
The unit of magnetic flux (Weber) is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: Magnetic flux Φ = BA has units of T·m² = Weber (Wb).

questions.text: ¹⁷₇N and ¹⁸₈O are examples of:
questions.explanation: ¹⁴₇N: neutrons = 14-7 = 7; ¹⁶₈O: neutrons = 16-8 = 8. Wait — checking ¹⁷N: n=10, ¹⁸O: n=10. Same neutrons → isotones.

questions.text: The force between two charges is 5.70 N when q₁ = 26 μC and q₂ = -47 μC. Their separation is:
A proton released in a 520 N/C field has speed after 48 ns of:
For a non-conducting infinite plane with charge density σ = 5 nC/m², the field on one side is:
A parallel-plate capacitor has circular plates of radius 8.2 cm and separation 1.3 mm. Its capacitance is approximately:
600 J of energy moves 9.36×10¹⁹ electrons between two points. The voltage is approximately:
An EMF is induced in a loop when:
questions.explanation: By Faraday's Law, EMF is induced whenever dΦ/dt ≠ 0.
options: The loop is stationary in a constant B field
The magnetic flux through the loop changes
Current flows through a nearby wire only
The resistance of the loop changes

questions.text: What is the charge on the proton?
questions.explanation: The proton has a charge of +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, equal in magnitude but opposite in sign to the electron.

questions.text: Materials in which charges can move freely are called:
questions.explanation: Conductors are materials in which electric charges can move about freely.

questions.text: For a large number of field lines originating from a charge, what does this indicate?
questions.explanation: The number of field lines originating from a charge should be proportional to the magnitude of the charge.

questions.text: What shape of Gaussian surface is most useful for a charge distribution with cylindrical symmetry?
questions.explanation: Cylindrical Gaussian surfaces exploit the cylindrical symmetry of line charges or coaxial cylinders.

questions.text: Energy stored per unit volume (energy density) in a capacitor is:
questions.explanation: Energy density u = ½ε₀E² applies to any electric field regardless of its source.

questions.text: 840 coulombs pass through a plane in 2 minutes. The current is:
The work done by a magnetic force on a moving charge is:
questions.explanation: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity, so it does no work on the charge.

questions.text: Cathode rays have:
questions.explanation: Cathode rays are electrons, which have both mass (9.11×10⁻³¹ kg) and charge (-1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C).

questions.text: One coulomb of charge is the amount that flows when a current of 1 ampere flows for:
questions.explanation: By definition: 1 C = 1 A × 1 s.

questions.text: The work done in moving a charge q through potential difference V is:
questions.explanation: By definition of potential difference: V = W/q → W = qV.

questions.text: A velocity selector uses crossed E and B fields to select particles where:
questions.explanation: When electric and magnetic forces balance: qE = qvB → v = E/B (independent of charge and mass).

questions.text: In ¹⁷⁵₇₁Lu, the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons respectively are:
questions.explanation: Z=71 (protons=electrons=71); neutrons = A-Z = 175-71 = 104.

questions.text: The electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is zero because:
questions.explanation: Free electrons in conductors rearrange until the internal field is zero — this is electrostatic equilibrium.
options: Free charges redistribute until E=0 inside

questions.text: The spherical capacitor formula C = 4πε₀ab/(b-a) applies to:
questions.explanation: The spherical capacitor consists of two concentric conducting spheres with inner radius a and outer radius b.
options: Two concentric spheres of radii a and b

questions.text: In the color code system, the color Orange represents the digit:
questions.explanation: Standard resistor color code: Black=0, Brown=1, Red=2, Orange=3, Yellow=4, Green=5...

questions.text: The magnetic moment of a current loop is:
questions.explanation: The magnetic dipole moment m = IA, where I is current and A is the area of the loop.

questions.text: Isotopes of an element show the same __________ properties but different __________ properties.
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same Z (same electrons) → same chemical behavior, but different masses → different physical properties.

questions.text: The electric field between the plates of a parallel-plate capacitor is:
questions.explanation: Between the plates, contributions from both plates add: E = σ/(2ε₀) + σ/(2ε₀) = σ/ε₀.

questions.text: When traversing a resistor in the direction of the assumed current (using KVL), the voltage change is:
questions.explanation: Moving through a resistor in the direction of current flow gives a voltage DROP of -IR.

questions.text: Paramagnetism is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Paramagnetic materials are weakly attracted to magnets and lose magnetism when the external field is removed.
options: Weak attraction to magnets, loses magnetism without external field

questions.text: Atomic weight is defined as:
questions.explanation: Atomic weight = Σ(Wᵢ × Xᵢ)/Σ(Xᵢ), averaging isotope masses by percent occurrence.
options: The mass number of the most common isotope
The average of the masses of all isotopes weighted by their natural abundance
The mass of one mole of atoms

questions.text: The charge on a neutron is:
questions.explanation: Neutrons are electrically neutral — they carry zero net charge.

questions.text: Which formula gives the electric field on the axis of an electric dipole at large distance z?
questions.explanation: On the axis of a dipole far from it: E_z = 2kp/z³ = p/(2πε₀z³).

questions.text: Gauss's Law is most easily applied when the charge distribution has:
questions.explanation: Gauss's Law is most useful for high-symmetry distributions where E is constant over the Gaussian surface.

questions.text: The dielectric constant κ of vacuum/air is:
questions.explanation: The dielectric constant of vacuum (and approximately air) is κ = 1 (the reference value).

questions.text: A wire has resistivity ρ, length 2L, and cross-sectional area A/2. Compared to a wire of length L and area A, its resistance is:
questions.explanation: R = ρL/A. New R = ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4ρL/A = 4R_original.

questions.text: Mutual inductance M between two coils is defined by:
questions.explanation: Mutual inductance: EMF₁ = -M(dI₂/dt), the EMF induced in coil 1 due to changing current in coil 2.

questions.text: Deuterium (²H) differs from protium (¹H) in that it has:
questions.explanation: Deuterium (²₁H) has Z=1 (same protons and electrons as H), but A=2, so it has 1 neutron vs 0 for protium.

questions.text: The electric field at a point where a 5 μC charge experiences a force of 2 N is:
Three 25 μF capacitors connected in parallel across 4200 V. Total charge through meter is:
questions.explanation: Each capacitor: q = CV = 25×10⁻⁶ × 4200 = 0.105 C. Total = 3 × 0.105 = 0.315 C.

questions.text: The magnetic field inside a toroid (donut-shaped solenoid) with N turns, mean radius R, and current I is:
questions.explanation: Using Ampere's Law for a toroid: B = μ₀NI/(2πR).

questions.text: The Rutherford model proposed in 1911 failed because it predicted that electrons would:
questions.explanation: In Rutherford's model, accelerating electrons should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, making atoms unstable.
options: Spiral inward and lose energy (unstable atom)

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes electric charge?
questions.explanation: Conservation of charge: the total electric charge of an isolated system remains constant.
options: Charge can be created from nothing
The total charge of an isolated system is conserved

questions.text: A disk of radius 2.5 cm with surface charge density 5.3 μC/m² produces a field at z = 12 cm on its axis of approximately:
questions.explanation: Using E = σ/(2ε₀)[1 - z/√(z²+R²)] with given values yields E ≈ 629 N/C.

questions.text: A ball hanging at θ = 30° from a vertical charged sheet has charge 2×10⁻⁸ C and mass 1 mg. The surface charge density σ is:
questions.explanation: F_elec = mg tan30° = 5.7×10⁻⁶ N; E = F/q = 285 N/C; σ = 2ε₀E ≈ 5.0 nC/m².

questions.text: Energy stored in 1 m³ of air in the 'fair weather' electric field of 150 V/m is:
Resistivity ρ of a material has SI units of:
questions.explanation: From R = ρL/A: ρ = RA/L has units of Ω·m²/m = Ω·m.

questions.text: Diamagnetic materials are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Diamagnetic materials (like bismuth, copper) are weakly repelled by magnetic fields.

questions.text: Be²⁺ is isoelectronic with which species?
questions.explanation: Be²⁺ has Z=4, loses 2 electrons → 2 electrons total. Li⁺ has Z=3, loses 1 electron → 2 electrons. Both have 2 electrons.

questions.text: Coulomb's Law applies to:
questions.explanation: Coulomb's Law applies exactly to point charges and to spherically symmetric charge distributions (treated as point charges).
options: Point charges only (or spherical charge distributions)

questions.text: The electric field strength at a distance r from a point charge is proportional to:
questions.explanation: E = kq/r² — the electric field from a point charge falls off as the inverse square of distance.

questions.text: The right-hand rule for magnetic force F = qv × B states:
questions.explanation: For F = qv × B: point fingers along v, curl them toward B, thumb indicates F for a positive charge.
options: Point fingers in direction of v, curl toward B; thumb points in direction of F for positive q
Point thumb in direction of B; curl fingers give F
Point fingers toward B; curl toward v; thumb gives F
Wrap fingers around the wire in the direction of current

questions.text: The mass number always has a:
questions.explanation: Mass number A = protons + neutrons, always a whole number. Atomic weight may be decimal.

questions.text: What does ∮B·dA = 0 imply about magnetic fields?
questions.explanation: ∮B·dA = 0 (Gauss's Law for magnetism) means the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero — no magnetic monopoles exist.

questions.text: If a dielectric with κ = 3 is inserted between capacitor plates while charge is held constant, the voltage:
questions.explanation: C increases by κ=3; since q is constant and V = q/C, V decreases to V/3.

questions.text: The color Silver as the 4th band of a resistor indicates a tolerance of:
questions.explanation: Silver tolerance band = ±10%. Gold = ±5%. No band = ±20%.

questions.text: The flux through a loop of area A = 0.1 m² in a field B = 2 T at angle 30° to the normal is:
An isotone of ³²₁₆S (sulfur-32) would be an atom with:
questions.explanation: S-32: neutrons = 32-16 = 16. An isotone has the same number of neutrons (16) but a different element (different Z).

questions.text: The concept of an electric field was introduced to:
questions.explanation: The electric field concept was introduced to explain how charges exert forces on each other through space (action at a distance).
options: Describe how charges influence the space around them without requiring direct contact

questions.text: In a circuit with a 9 V battery and total resistance 9 Ω, the current drawn from the battery is:
